Retrieval-augmented generation systems face a deceptively hard problem when retrieved text says one thing and the model's trained weights encode something different: the model must decide which source of "knowledge" to trust, and that decision interacts badly with how facts decompose into sub-facts. The central question is: at what granularity does a model's compositionality break down — meaning, can it correctly combine a retrieved atomic fact ("X was appointed in 2021") with parametric relational knowledge ("X's role oversees Y") to produce a correctly updated inference ("Y is currently overseen by someone appointed in 2021"), or does the contradiction at one level corrupt reasoning at adjacent levels? Key concepts here are parametric knowledge (facts baked into weights during training), contextual override (the model deferring to retrieved text), specificity levels (atomic facts vs. relational structures vs. multi-hop chains), and compositional consistency (whether locally correct updates propagate correctly through dependent inferences). A beginner assumes the failure mode is simple — either the model ignores the retrieved fact or it accepts it — but an expert worries about something subtler: partial override, where the model accepts a retrieved fact at the surface level but its downstream reasoning silently reverts to parametric assumptions, producing answers that are locally plausible but globally incoherent. The practical danger is that these failures are nearly invisible in standard evaluation because each individual output sentence can look correct while the composed inference is wrong.

NEXT: When a retrieved fact contradicts parametric knowledge, what determines whether the model's override is shallow (surface acknowledgment only) versus deep (propagating through dependent inferences)?

The depth of override appears to be governed primarily by attentional distance: how many reasoning hops separate the retrieved fact from the dependent inference, and whether intervening tokens re-activate parametric associations before the model reaches the conclusion. Mallen et al. (2023) in the PopQA work showed that models like GPT-3 and OPT defer to context reliably for direct lookups but revert to parametric defaults as soon as the question requires even one relational step beyond the retrieved span — the override literally doesn't survive a single compositional join. A second determinant is entity familiarity: Longpre et al. (2021) in their entity substitution experiments found that high-frequency entities in training (major world capitals, celebrity names) resist override more stubbornly than low-frequency ones, because the parametric signal for familiar entities is stronger and effectively competes with the context signal during decoding. A third, less obvious factor is syntactic embedding depth of the contradiction — a retrieved fact stated as a main clause ("X is now CEO") overrides more reliably than the same fact buried in a subordinate clause or presupposition, suggesting the model's context-reading is sensitive to surface prominence in ways that have nothing to do with logical relevance. The practical consequence, documented in RALM probing work by Shi et al. (2023), is that you can construct inputs where the model correctly paraphrases the retrieved fact in one sentence and then contradicts it two sentences later by reasoning from parametric memory — the override was never written into the working representation, only into the output surface.

The evidence strongly suggests fine-tuning teaches surface behavior rather than reducing parametric resistance at the representational level. Longpre et al.'s fine-tuning experiments showed accuracy improvements on direct contradictions but the gains were disproportionately concentrated on low-familiarity entities — for high-familiarity entities, fine-tuning on contradictory contexts produced models that stated the retrieved fact correctly while still generating downstream inferences consistent with the original parametric belief, exactly the shallow-override signature. More mechanistic evidence comes from Rome/ROME-style editing work (Meng et al., 2022): when causal tracing is applied after editing, the MLP layers storing the original factual association remain active and still route through to later layers — the edit patches the output but doesn't silence the source, which is structurally identical to what fine-tuning on retrieved contradictions likely does at scale. Geiger et al.'s interchange intervention work further suggests that fine-tuning changes which representations get read at the output layer without changing the underlying representational geometry — the parametric knowledge is still there, still computed, just down-weighted in the final linear combination rather than suppressed. The practical diagnostic is counterfactual consistency testing: a model with genuine deep override should answer consistently whether the contradiction is stated once or five times, foregrounded or backgrounded; models that have only learned surface behavior show dramatic sensitivity to that kind of presentational variation, which several RLHF-tuned models do when probed this way. This means evaluation benchmarks that test single-hop retrieval fidelity will systematically overestimate how thoroughly a fine-tuned model has actually resolved the parametric-contextual conflict.

Yes, and this is one of the more unsettling empirical findings in the space. Shi et al. (2023) in "Large Language Models Can Be Easily Distracted by Irrelevant Context" demonstrated that adding semantically irrelevant sentences near a retrieved fact — sentences that don't contradict or modify it — significantly degraded the model's ability to use that fact correctly, with accuracy dropping 30+ percentage points on some arithmetic and reasoning tasks; the distraction effectively re-weighted attention away from the override and toward parametric priors. More directly, Xu et al. (2023) in counterfactual robustness probing showed that simply rephrasing the retrieved context from declarative to interrogative framing, or embedding it in a hypothetical ("suppose it were the case that X..."), was sufficient to collapse the override on high-familiarity entities — the semantic content is identical but the pragmatic framing signals uncertainty, and the model appears to use that signal as a license to revert. Jailbreak-adjacent work on factual suppression (Hernandez et al., 2023 on ROME follow-ups) found that soft prompt perturbations of as few as 5 tokens prepended to an edited context could recover the pre-edit answer with over 60% reliability, suggesting the parametric representation is not just active but remains preferentially accessible under mild distributional shift. The mechanism appears to be that fine-tuning and in-context override both operate on relatively shallow output-routing circuits, while the parametric fact is encoded redundantly across many MLP layers — so any perturbation that slightly disrupts the routing circuit falls back on the more robust distributed representation. The security implication is serious: a RAG system that passes standard retrieval-fidelity benchmarks can be made to ignore its retrieved context and hallucinate parametric answers through prompt perturbations that look innocuous to a human reviewer.

The asymmetry is real and sharp: models handle novel retrieved facts substantially better than contradictory ones, which isolates the failure as interference rather than integration capacity. Mallen et al.'s PopQA results make this concrete — for entities below a frequency threshold where essentially no parametric encoding exists, retrieval accuracy was near-ceiling (above 80%), while for high-familiarity entities with strong parametric encodings, retrieval accuracy under contradiction dropped to ranges competitive with just ignoring the context entirely. This asymmetry tells you that the compositional machinery itself — the attention patterns and MLP routing that read retrieved text and chain it into inference — is not the broken component; the model can compose with retrieved facts when there's no competition. The failure originates specifically in the conflict resolution circuit, or more precisely in the absence of a robust one: the model has no dedicated mechanism to suppress a parametric encoding when context contradicts it, so composition proceeds but draws on a mixture of the retrieved fact and the residual parametric signal, producing the partial-override failures described earlier. Hase et al. (2023) on model editing localization sharpened this further by showing that even when an edit successfully changes a direct-query answer, multi-hop inferences downstream of that edit remain anchored to the pre-edit parametric state — novel-fact insertions don't show this asymmetry because there's no pre-edit state competing, confirming the problem is specifically interference at the compositional join, not the join mechanism itself. The practical implication is that retrieval systems should be more concerned about what the model already knows about retrieved entities than about retrieval quality per se — a perfectly retrieved contradictory fact can be worse than no retrieval at all if it triggers partial override that corrupts otherwise-reliable parametric reasoning.

There is promising but incomplete evidence that this is feasible. Slobodkin et al. (2023) and related probing work have shown that linear probes trained on intermediate layer representations can predict, with above-chance accuracy, whether a model will defer to context or revert to parametric memory — meaning the "which source wins" decision is represented in the residual stream before it manifests in output tokens, and is in principle detectable. Hernandez et al.'s causal tracing work provides the mechanistic grounding: when a familiar entity appears in context alongside a contradicting retrieved fact, both the contextual attribute binding (primarily in early attention layers) and the parametric attribute (in mid-to-late MLP layers) produce distinguishable activation signatures in the residual stream, and their relative magnitudes at the final token position before generation correlates with which one surfaces in the output. The practical challenge is that this detection requires knowing what the parametric encoding of the entity is in order to construct the right probe direction — you need to separately elicit the model's parametric answer, compute its representation, and then check for that direction's presence during RAG inference, which adds latency and requires a clean parametric-elicitation prompt that doesn't itself get contaminated by the retrieved context. Jiaoda Li et al. (2023) on "inference-time intervention" showed you can go further than detection: steering vectors applied at the right layer can shift the balance toward contextual over parametric, with roughly 20-30% override improvement on counterfactual datasets, though with degradation on cases where the parametric answer was actually correct. The deeper problem is that simultaneous activation doesn't always mean conflict — sometimes both representations genuinely agree, and the probe can't yet reliably distinguish "both active and consistent" from "both active and competing," which limits its precision as a pre-decoding alarm.

The degradation is real and has been measured. Li et al.'s inference-time intervention results show that steering vectors tuned for contradiction robustness do reduce accuracy on novel-fact cases, though the magnitude depends heavily on intervention strength — moderate interventions show 5-10% degradation on novel facts while recovering 20-30% on contradictory ones, but aggressive interventions flatten the model's ability to integrate genuinely new information almost entirely, essentially converting it into a parametric-only system that ignores context. This confirms a fundamental tension, but its structure is more specific than a simple robustness-sensitivity tradeoff: what's actually in conflict are two different reading strategies — skeptical reading (treat context as a potential correction to be verified against internal state) versus receptive reading (treat context as ground truth and suppress internal state) — and a uniform steering vector forces one strategy globally when the optimal strategy is fact-dependent. Asai et al.'s SELF-RAG (2023) attempted to escape this by training the model to emit a reflection token predicting whether retrieved content is relevant and whether it conflicts with parametric knowledge, conditionally applying different processing — in effect, routing to skeptical vs. receptive mode per-fact rather than globally, which recovered much of the novel-fact performance while maintaining contradiction robustness. The tension reveals something deeper: the model has no reliable internal signal for its own parametric uncertainty, meaning it can't easily self-diagnose when its parametric encoding is strong-but-wrong versus absent, which is precisely the condition that would allow intelligent routing. Until models can accurately represent their own parametric confidence at entity-attribute granularity — not just output-level calibration but representation-level uncertainty — any global intervention will face this tradeoff, because the intervention can't condition on information the model doesn't reliably have.

The evidence points uncomfortably toward learned surface behavior. When Asai et al. evaluate SELF-RAG's reflection tokens, the evaluation is almost entirely on in-distribution tasks where the model has seen similar conflict patterns during training — there is no systematic test of whether the reflection tokens remain calibrated under the kinds of presentational perturbations (subordinate clause embedding, hypothetical framing, irrelevant distractor sentences) that reliably break standard override, which is exactly the test that would distinguish genuine internal signal from surface pattern matching. Indirect evidence that they're surface behaviors comes from the probing asymmetry: if reflection tokens tracked genuine representational conflict, you'd expect them to correlate with the residual stream signature that Hernandez et al. identified as the parametric-contextual competition signal — but no published work has verified this correlation, and the architectural position of reflection token generation (at the output layer, after the residual stream has already been collapsed to a distribution) makes it structurally unlikely they're reading deep representational conflict rather than surface textual cues. More damningly, Yoran et al. (2023) in "Making Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Robust to Irrelevant Context" showed that models trained to detect and filter conflicting context learn highly lexical conflict signals — negation words, temporal markers, explicit contradiction phrases — and fail when conflict is expressed through implication or presupposition rather than overt markers, exactly the surface-pattern signature. The deeper structural problem is that reflection tokens are generated autoregressively from the same representational substrate that produces the answer, meaning they're subject to the same parametric pull — a model that would generate the wrong answer due to parametric dominance would likely also generate a reflection token saying no conflict exists, because both decisions draw on the same corrupted weighting. This makes SELF-RAG's architecture self-undermining in precisely the cases where conflict detection matters most: high-familiarity entities with strong parametric encodings are the ones most likely to produce both a wrong answer and a falsely confident "no conflict" reflection token simultaneously.
